topic_tag: river beetle colony after a flood
passage: Each spring flightless beetles nest on a gravel bar in a western river, eating the seeds of low plants there and walking across a narrow gravel spit to mate with colonies on the bank. This year the flood crested no higher than usual, and the spit came back. The water filled the burrows of the bank ants that cross the spit each summer to carry off larvae, no ants reached the bar all season, and in July it held more young than in any year of the survey. After surveying the bar in July, one ecologist reported that the year's flood had ______ the colony.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The flood drowned out the ants that raid the larvae, and the colony then raised a record number of young, so the flood protected it: it "sheltered" the colony. "Stranded" fails because the spit came back; "starved" fails because a colony raising record numbers was not short of food; "swamped" fails because an ordinary crest left the colony thriving.

topic_tag: lava flow and a valley river
passage: About nine thousand years ago, a tongue of lava poured into a narrow mountain valley and hardened across the floor where a river had wound in wide loops toward a lake. As it cooled, the lava split along a single crack that runs as true as a surveyor's line for four miles down the middle of the flow. The river found that crack and cut its trench into it, and fish from the lake still swim up the trench each spring to spawn where the river leaves the hills. Mapping the valley today, geologists conclude that the lava ______ the river.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The river now follows a crack that runs as true as a surveyor's line for four miles, where it once wound in wide loops: the lava "straightened" it. "Swallowed" fails because the river cut an open trench; "trapped" fails because fish still swim up from the lake, so the river still flows into it; "sidetracked" fails because it still reaches the same lake.

passage: Farmers in one northern valley once built hundreds of dry stone walls, and today the walls are coated with lichens, slow-growing crusts of fungus and algae. The commonest crust on the walls is a species otherwise known only from bark in the oak forest that covered the valley until it was cleared four centuries ago. It has never spread to new stone, growing only on walls built from boulders hauled out of that forest's floor, and each decade a few more of its old patches flake away without being replaced. In her field guide, one botanist describes these crusts as a living ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The crust survives only on stones from a forest that is gone, never spreads, and slowly disappears, so it is a remnant of that vanished forest: a living "vestige." "Sentinel" fails because nothing in its slow loss signals a change in conditions; "timeline" fails because patches that flake away and are never replaced record no steady time; "scaffold" fails because patches that flake off leave nothing for other plants.

passage: Since 1950, survey crews have returned every summer to an eight-kilometer mountain glacier whose lower end lies under a thick blanket of fallen rock. Through the warm 1950s the front pulled back a little farther each summer, a full kilometer in all, leaving a strip of raw gravel. A run of snowy winters began in 1959, and the front pushed forward over that same gravel, flattening the young willows that had sprouted there; since 1966 its position has not shifted by more than a few meters. Looking back over seventy years of those surveys, one glaciologist described the glacier's loss of ice as ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The glacier lost ice through the 1950s, then advanced back over the ground it had lost and has stayed there since 1966, so the loss was "short-lived." "Sporadic" fails because the front pulled back a little each summer; "slight" fails because it lost a full kilometer; "stealthy" fails because the retreat left raw gravel in plain view.

passage: Each autumn several thousand snow geese fly some three thousand kilometers from the northern tundra to coastal marshes, and ordinarily the whole population lifts off within a few days of one another in mid-October. That year the flocks set off together on their usual date, after the first storms had already glazed the southern prairies with ice. Banded birds turned up all winter on a chain of open lakes halfway along the route, and counters on the marshes, who usually log thousands of arrivals, logged almost none at all. In her account of one season, an ornithologist wrote that a string of early storms had ______ the geese's migration.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The geese left on time but spent the winter on lakes halfway along the route and never reached the marshes, so the storms "truncated" the migration. "Staggered" fails because the flocks set off together; "spurred" fails because they left on their usual date; "swelled" fails because almost no birds arrived at the marshes.

topic_tag: early measurements of heat from the ocean floor
passage: In the 1930s, two small research teams lowered thermometers into holes drilled in the seabed to measure how much heat escapes from the ocean floor. Heat leaking up along the drill pipes made both readings about ten times too low, and the low numbers seemed to confirm what most geologists already believed, that the ocean floor was cold and inert. For three decades, grant committees cited them when turning down proposals to study the seabed's heat, until a 1962 survey found the leak. Historians of geology now regard those two measurements as ______ in the history of their field.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Wrong readings confirmed a mistaken view and were used for thirty years to block research, so they held the field back: "setbacks." "Touchstones" fails because values ten times too low are no standard; "watersheds" fails because they confirmed the existing view rather than changing it; "sideshows" fails because they shaped funding decisions for three decades.

topic_tag: a drought and a pine forest
passage: For centuries pines have covered a dry foothill ridge, with a few scrub oaks scattered among them, and in the 1950s a seven-year drought struck it. During the drought the rings narrowed sharply, and within five years they had widened to their old breadth again. When dry years returned in the 1970s, the ridge pines laid down rings almost as wide as in a wet year, while pines on a wetter slope across the valley, which had never known drought, laid down their narrowest rings on record. Reading the tree rings decades later, one forest ecologist concluded that the drought had ______ the pines on the ridge.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: In the next drought, the pines that had been through the 1950s grew almost normally while untested pines nearby barely grew, so the drought made them hardier: it "toughened" them. "Stunted" fails because their rings widened to their old breadth; "thinned" fails because the same trees are tracked through the 1970s; "sidelined" fails because they kept growing strongly.

passage: In 1838 a provincial assembly passed a law governing disputes between landowners and the tenant farmers who rented their fields. It created a county board as the only lawful place to contest a rent, and required the landowner to answer at the board's next sitting. Sheriffs' reports that had recorded dozens of blocked roads and burned hayricks in 1837 record almost none after 1839, while the board's minutes list hundreds of petitions a year, close to the number of incidents the sheriffs once counted, until both lists dwindle after grain prices fell. Looking back, one historian argued that the law had ______ the conflict it was written to end.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Roadblocks and burnings gave way to roughly as many petitions before the new board, so the law "channeled" the conflict into a new course. "Deferred" fails because landowners had to answer at the next sitting. "Escalated" fails because the number of petitions matched the earlier incidents, and "entrenched" fails because both lists dwindled once grain prices fell.

topic_tag: sociology of a weekly town market
passage: A sociologist spent three years observing the Saturday market of a small farming town, whose stalls sold much the same goods every week. The town had no newspaper, no telephone exchange, and no employment office. The sociologist found that farmers left word at particular stalls of jobs, strayed animals, and land to let, that the stallholders sorted these notices by village and handed each to the next customer from that village, and that most hired hands in the district had found their places this way. By the 1950s, the sociologist concluded, the market mattered to the town less for its trade than as its principal ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: With no newspaper or employment office, notices left at the stalls were sorted and handed on to the right villages, so the market served as the town's "clearinghouse." "Forum" fails because the notices were sorted and passed along, not debated. "Archive" fails because the information was current and kept moving, and "battleground" fails because nothing suggests conflict.

topic_tag: an early modern agreement between port cities
passage: In 1724 two rival port cities signed an agreement on the use of each other's harbors. It was signed at a three-day feast after a procession of both councils through each city, and its text consists of pledges of friendship with no fees, schedules, or penalties. Harbor logs for the following decade show the same tolls charged, the same ships turned away, and the same seizures of each other's vessels as in the decade before. Having compared the surviving drafts, one historian judged the final agreement to be above all ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A feast and procession produced pledges that changed nothing in the harbors, so the agreement was above all "ceremonial." "Candid" fails because its pledges of friendship sat beside continuing seizures. "Expedient" fails because it met no practical need, since nothing changed, and "exhaustive" fails because it set no rules at all.

topic_tag: a craft guild and a city's glass trade
passage: In 1480 the glassmakers of a river city formed a guild with its own officers and rules. After a workshop fire spread across three streets in 1491, its officers had the council forbid any furnace within the walls and grant the guild one small island downstream. Tax rolls list forty workshops on that island in 1530, paying about the same duty on finished glass as the forty in the city had paid in 1480, and glass was still the plain cup of the ordinary household. According to one economic historian, within fifty years the guild had ______ the city's glass trade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Furnaces were barred from the city and the workshops ended up on one island, so the guild "confined" the trade. "Doubled" fails because the duty stayed about the same. "Elevated" fails because glass remained a plain household cup, and "abandoned" fails because forty workshops kept working on the island.

topic_tag: a shared school and a rivalry between towns
passage: Two towns in a narrow valley had quarreled since 1870 over who should pay for the bridge between them. In 1924 they opened a single high school for both. Its history teachers retold the bridge quarrel every year with a drowned mayor and a stolen church bell, neither found in the 1870 court papers or any newspaper of the time. Its teams always mixed students from both towns and its events were free, and surveys in the 1930s found graduates more hostile to the other town than their parents were. A local historian later wrote that the new school had ______ the rivalry between the two towns.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Teachers retold the quarrel each year with events found in no record, so the school "embellished" the rivalry. "Defused" fails because graduates were more hostile than their parents. "Formalized" fails because the teams mixed the towns, and "commercialized" fails because its events were free.

passage: In 1893, during a deep economic slump, a mid-sized industrial city began giving aid to families out of work. Its clerk modeled it on the "friendly visitor" scheme that reform clubs in every large city were then praising in their journals, assigning each family a volunteer who called weekly, and that winter's charity ball was given in the scheme's honor. A family applied once at the town hall, the city's accounts show it paying more per family than neighboring cities, and the program ran in that form until 1920. In her history of the city, one scholar described its relief program of the 1890s as above all ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Copied from a scheme reform clubs everywhere were praising, and celebrated with a charity ball, the program was above all "fashionable." "Frugal" fails because it paid more per family than neighbors. "Cumbersome" fails because a family applied once, and "experimental" fails because it copied an established scheme and ran unchanged until 1920.

passage: In 1931 a touring company staged a new version of a little-known seventeenth-century tragedy in which a queen gives up the soldier she loves and dies of grief. Its director found the queen's long speeches of doubt slow, and he struck them, though they are the only place where she weighs her throne against her love. What remained, played in the author's sequence, was a brisk run of duels and deaths, and patrons were out in good time for supper, dry-eyed and unable to say why the queen had died. One reviewer who knew the original text well wrote that the production had ______ the play.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Striking the only speeches in which the queen weighs her choice left audiences "unable to say why the queen had died," so the production "gutted" the play. "Lengthened" fails because patrons were out in good time for supper; "jumbled" fails because the scenes kept the author's sequence; "lampooned" fails because the audience left puzzled, not amused.

passage: Many of the portraits a painter made in the last decade of her career include areas of gold leaf, and those late canvases are now her most studied. The gold first appears in three portraits she delivered in the winter of 1960, when a dock strike had halted shipments of yellow pigment. X-rays show each background half-painted in ochre and then covered with uneven scraps of leaf of the kind framers throw away, laid on so fast that brush hairs are trapped beneath them; the sitters, old friends, hung the pictures in their front rooms. One critic who has examined them closely describes the painter's use of gold as ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Gold appears when a strike cut off her pigment, laid over half-finished backgrounds in hasty scraps, so its use was "improvised." "Ingrained" fails because it first appears in 1960; "incidental" fails because it covers whole backgrounds; "ironic" fails because the sitters, her friends, displayed the pictures proudly.

topic_tag: a small press and a poetry movement
passage: Early in the last century, a one-room press in a river town printed poetry in editions of a few hundred copies. In 1909 its editor printed a pamphlet calling for poems in the plain speech of the river towns, about farm work and flood seasons rather than nightingales. The press burned the next year, when the poets who would write exactly such poems a decade later were still schoolchildren, and none of them saw the pamphlet until a librarian found it in 1930. One historian of the town's literary life argues that the press ______ the plain-spoken regional poetry that flourished there in the 1920s.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The 1909 pamphlet called for the very poetry that arrived a decade later, so the press "heralded" the movement. "Housed" fails because the press burned in 1910; "hindered" fails because the poets were still schoolchildren then, so it obstructed nothing; "guided" fails because none of them saw the pamphlet until 1930.

topic_tag: a harbor painting in a provincial museum
passage: A small canvas of a harbor at dawn, painted in 1874, hangs in a provincial museum among the painter's other early work. Until that spring he had painted in the smooth, polished manner taught at the academy, and the harbor began that way too. Halfway through, he scraped the whole canvas down and repainted it in short, broken strokes of unmixed color, a method he had seen nowhere; he signed it openly, and nothing he painted in the forty years after returns to the polished manner. Historians of the period have long called the canvas the painter's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The canvas where he abandoned the academic manner, never to return to it, is his "landmark." "Hoax" fails because he signed it openly; "homage" fails because the method was one he had seen nowhere; "hybrid" fails because he scraped the whole canvas down, replacing the old manner rather than blending it.

passage: In 1958 a jazz singer published a memoir of her forty years onstage, years that included a divorce, a bankruptcy, and a long feud with the band she had founded. Readers who knew her story waited for the divorce and the bankruptcy and found one sentence noting that in 1949 she "moved to a smaller flat." Her former bandmates appear only as "the band," and the prose, which she revised over ten years, is careful and exact, though every chapter ends at her dressing-room door. Reviewing the book in a literary weekly, one critic called it ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Reducing her divorce and bankruptcy to a move to "a smaller flat" and stopping every chapter at her dressing-room door make the memoir "guarded." "Gracious" fails because her bandmates go unnamed and uncredited as "the band"; "gritty" fails because the hard years get one euphemistic sentence; "glib" fails because the prose was revised over ten years.

passage: When a poet died in 1902, she left 212 untitled poems loose in a desk drawer, with no instructions for what should become of them. Her niece, a minister's wife, printed all 212 in the order she found them, as a plain book of one poem to a page. When the manuscripts resurfaced in 1990, scholars found that the poet's "God, if there is one" had become "God, who surely is," and that a dozen love poems addressed to a woman had been readdressed to "my brother." Scholars agree that the niece who prepared the first published collection ______ the poems.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Turning doubt into faith and readdressing love poems so they read respectably means the niece "laundered" them. "Grouped" fails because she kept the order she found them in; "illustrated" fails because it was a plain book; "interrupted" fails because each poem had its own page.

passage: In 2015 a small software firm began working with independent restaurants in one mid-sized city, where several national delivery apps already operated. Its software let each restaurant take orders on its own website, which none of the national apps then allowed. Within three years every one of those apps had built a near copy, while restaurants using the firm's version went on paying only a flat yearly license, keeping every diner's payment themselves, and settling their own complaints. By 2018, most of the city's restaurant owners spoke of the firm as their trade's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The firm offered something no app had allowed and was later copied by all of them, so owners saw it as their trade's "pioneer." "Middleman" fails because restaurants kept every diner's payment themselves. "Publicist" fails because restaurants paid only a license for software, not for promotion, and "referee" fails because restaurants settled their own complaints.

passage: Last spring, the council of one river town replaced the property tax that paid for trash pickup with a monthly fee charged to each household. A cost study attached to every bill showed that the charge, twenty dollars for a mansion and twenty for a one-room apartment, exactly covered the cost of pickups beginning the month after the vote. A retired couple on a fixed income thus paid as much as the factory owner up the hill, out of an income a tenth the size. Several council members objected that the fee, as written, was ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Because rich and poor households paid the same amount, the fee took a far larger share from smaller incomes, so it was "regressive." "Punitive" fails because it exactly covered the cost of pickup. "Retroactive" fails because it covered pickups beginning the month after the vote, and "opaque" fails because a cost study was attached to every bill.
